The strange world of sight
 
Seeing is believing, it is said. But, asks Richard Gregory, could it be the other way round?
 
A Two of the great British men of the 17th century, the philosopher John Locke and the physicist Isaac Newton, were both aware that objects are not coloured, and that against all appearances light is not coloured either. This is still not generally recognised even now, 400 years later, because it seems so implausible. Yet it tells us something very important — that perceptions are not identical with what we perceive, and may be very different. The most accurate historical account of perception is that of the 19th-century German scientist Hermann von Helmholtz. However, it was ridiculed at the time. Von Helmholtz thought that perceptions are unconscious inferences we make based on a combination of clues provided by the eyes and other senses, and knowledge of the world. This idea of unconscious inference for perception preceded, by several years, the psychoanalyst Freud's notion of the unconscious, which was also initially treated with derision because it undermined the notion of humans as pre-eminently rational beings who could be held responsible for their actions and awarded blame or praise accordingly.
 
B Crucially, perception of the present depends on rich, though of course not always correct or appropriate, knowledge from the past. We interpret sense data (what we hear, touch, taste, see and smell) from the present according to what we already know. This raises the question: if we see the present through memory, why aren't past and present confused? The pioneering Russian neurologist Alexander Luria described the case of Mr S, who had a remarkable memory. However, it was prone to just such confusions, for example mistaking seeing his clock for remembering it, and so failing to get up in the morning. This suggests that perhaps an important function of perception is to underline the present. Individual perceptions have a vividness that is rare for memories, which might be how we are able to separate them. Try this: look at something for a few seconds, and then shut your eyes and visualise it in memory. You will almost certainly find that the memory is pale by comparison with the perception. Perhaps this is why past and present are not normally confused. Luria's Mr S had exceptionally vivid memories, and rich synaesthesia (experiencing perceptions from another sense as well as the one being stimulated, such as musical notes experienced as colours), which may be why he confused seeing with having seen.
 
C The complexity of processes involved in how we see first impressed itself on me 45 years ago. With my colleague Jean Wallace, I studied the rare case of Sydney Bradford, a man who had been born blind but, through a corneal graft at the age of 52, suddenly found himself able to see. Almost immediately after the operation he was able to 'see' but he could only see those things that he already knew about, having experienced them through touch. It was his touch memories that enabled him to perceive them with his eyes. When Bradford was first taken to the zoo, he proved utterly unable to see an elephant as he had no knowledge to make sense of his perceptions. The more recent case in California of Mike May, who was also born blind, is similar. Since his operation, his sight has gradually improved as he learns to see, for example, by understanding how shadows represent depth and tell us about the shape of things. Some of the consequences of May's new-found vision were less happy. He had been a champion blind skier, but following the operation, he would have to shut his eyes while skiing to block out what he now found was a terrifying sight.
 
D But acceptance of this intimate connection between memory and perception, even though it was first noticed in the 17th century, has been slow in brain science. Despite the fact that state-of-the-art brain imaging shows that perception animates parts of the brain associated with both present information and memory, most research on memory and perception is still undertaken as if these were separate processes. Seeing used to be thought of as taking place only in the eyes, and in quite specialised brain regions; but now it seems that half the brain is occupied with seeing, requiring a lot of energy. Perhaps this is why we shut our eyes for a rest. It is not just extreme cases like Mike May, but also much more common errors of seeing — illusions — that can reveal the crucial role of memory in governing what we (think we) see. Perception depends on specific knowledge and probabilities. Our brains calculate the likelihood of what is out there, and when too far-fetched, perceptions are rejected. A dramatic and discomforting example is looking at the two sides of a face-mask. From the front it is a convex shape with the nose sticking out. Then if the mask is rotated, the back of the mask will be seen as convex, though we know that it must be concave. It is almost, if not quite, impossible to sketch the back of a hollow mask to look as it is — hollow. Science often learns from what does not happen: people not seeing a hollow face as hollow is the most revealing experiment on perception. The unsettling truth from brain science is that even people with no visual impairment see what, at some level, they expect to see, and often miss things as they really are.

Questions 27–30
Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 27–30 on your answer sheet.

Q27 Why does the writer refer to Locke and Newton in the first paragraph?

  • A to indicate that his article will cover several scientific fields
  • B to stress how much physics has changed in 400 years
  • C to persuade the reader to take him seriously
  • D to point out that his notions are not new

Q28 According to the writer, why was Freud's theory of the unconscious mocked?

  • A It was too complex for his contemporaries to understand.
  • B It involved criticism of the way people behaved in society.
  • C People felt that it devalued the accepted concept of humanity.
  • D People assumed that it was intended as a joke.

Q29 The writer describes Mr S failing to get up in order to demonstrate

  • A how realistic most people's memories are
  • B how hard it is to tell dreaming and waking apart
  • C how unusual it is to mistake a perception for a memory
  • D how valuable knowledge of the past can be

Q30 What point is the writer making in the text as a whole?

  • A Perception involves much more than the data collected by the eyes.
  • B Learning to see as an adult can be a time-consuming process.
  • C Science is failing to devote enough attention to sight.
  • D Human perception is remarkably reliable.
Questions 31–36
Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 31–36 on your answer sheet, write:

Q31 Sydney Bradford relied on recollections of objects he had been told about to help him see after his operation.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q32 People who only start to see as adults can learn to see as other people do in time.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q33 People who have gained their sight as adults find certain activities harder to do than before.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q34 It is evident now that sight involves the eyes and one particular area of the brain.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q35 The mask experiment is particularly useful in training people who are regaining their sight.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN

Q36 People with perfect vision can fail to interpret objects correctly under certain circumstances.

  • A YES
  • B NO
  • C NOT GIVEN
Questions 37–40
Complete the summary using the list of words, A-J, below.
Write the correct letter, A-J, in boxes 37–40 on your answer sheet.
The mask experiment

In this experiment, having looked at the front of a simple face-mask, subjects look at the reverse. However, the subjects are convinced that they are still looking at a mask which is in shape. They believe that the is poking out in the normal manner because that is what they are used to seeing. Attempting to make a of the mask in this orientation leads to the same problem. The subjects fail to see a concave form because of the they have that the features of a face stick out.

  • A back
  • B brain
  • C view
  • D round
  • E sight
  • F nose
  • G convex
  • H hollow
  • I drawing
  • J preconception

reference:
Q27

干扰 引用古人通常是为了说明观点的历史渊源，而非“为了涵盖多个学科”（A）或“物理学变化很大”（B）。

句子 (Paragraph A) “Two of the great British men of the 17th century... This is still not generally recognised even now... Yet it tells us something very important...”

解析 题目问第一段提到Locke和Newton是为了什么。原文A段指出这两位17世纪的大师早就意识到物体本身没有颜色，光也没有颜色，尽管这在400年后仍未被普遍认识，但这告诉我们一个重要道理。引用他们是为了指出这个观点并不新（notions are not new），早在17世纪就有了。

Q28

解析 题目问为什么Freud的无意识理论被嘲笑。原文A段末尾提到Freud的理论最初受到嘲笑（treated with derision），因为它“undermined the notion of humans as pre-eminently rational beings（破坏了人类作为卓越理性存在的概念）”，对应选项 C (devalued the accepted concept of humanity)。

干扰 “Undermined the notion” 对应 “devalued the accepted concept”。

句子 (Paragraph A) “...because it undermined the notion of humans as pre-eminently rational beings...”

Q29

解析 题目问描述Mr S没起床是为了证明什么。原文B段通过Mr S把“看到钟”误认为是“记得钟”从而没起床的例子，说明这种混淆对于他来说发生了，但这反过来暗示了对于普通人来说，知觉（perception）的生动性（vividness）使得我们通常能区分过去和现在。通过特例（Mr S）来反衬常态：即对于普通人来说，把知觉误认为是记忆是多么不寻常（unusual），或者说知觉和记忆通常是分得很开的，对应选项 C。

干扰 Mr S是特例，他的混淆说明了缺乏生动性区分的后果，反证了正常情况下这种错误是unusual的。

句子 (Paragraph B) “...prone to just such confusions... This suggests that perhaps an important function of perception is to underline the present... vividness that is rare for memories...”

Q30

句子 全文主旨，尤其是A段 “perceptions are unconscious inferences” 和 D段 “half the brain is occupied with seeing”。

解析 题目问全文的主旨是什么。文章反复强调感知不仅仅是眼睛接收数据（Looking at own familiar world / unconscious inferences / knowledge from the past / brain occupied），而是涉及大脑、记忆和推理的复杂过程，对应选项 A (Perception involves much more than the data collected by the eyes)。

干扰 C（科学忽视）只是D段提到的一点；D（感知可靠）被文中多次提到的错觉（illusions/errors）否定。

Q31

解析 题目说Bradford依靠**别人告诉他的（what he had been told）**记忆来看见东西。原文C段说他能看见是因为他有“touch memories（触觉记忆）”，通过触摸体验过，而非“别人告诉的”，题目与原文矛盾，选 NO。

干扰 “Touch memories” 不等于 “memories of what he had been told”。

句子 (Paragraph C) “It was his touch memories that enabled him to perceive them with his eyes.”

Q32

解析 题目说成年后开始看见的人能恢复到与正常人相似的视力（similar sight to normal people）。原文C段提到Mike May视力“gradually improved（逐渐改善）”，但也提到依然有困难（如滑雪时要闭眼），并未明确说能达到“与正常人相似”的程度，信息缺失，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 “Improved” 不代表 “similar to normal”。

句子 (Paragraph C) “Since his operation, his sight has gradually improved as he learns to see...”

Q33

解析 题目说恢复视力的人做某些活动比失明时更难（harder）。原文C段末尾提到Mike May作为盲人滑雪冠军，手术后不得不“shut his eyes while skiing（滑雪时闭上眼睛）”来阻挡恐惧的景象，暗示看见反而让他滑雪变得困难/恐惧，选 YES。

干扰 必须闭眼才能滑雪 = 睁眼（恢复视力后）更难/无法进行。

句子 (Paragraph C) “...he would have to shut his eyes while skiing to block out what he now found was a terrifying sight.”

Q34

干扰 “Half the brain” 反驳了 “one particular part”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “...but now it seems that half the brain is occupied with seeing...”

解析 题目说视觉涉及大脑的一个特定部分（one particular part）。原文D段说过去认为只涉及特定区域，但现在看来“half the brain is occupied with seeing（半个大脑都被视觉占据）”，而非“one particular part”，选 NO。

Q35

解析 题目说面具实验被用来**训练（train）**人们看东西。原文D段只说这是一个“revealing experiment on perception（关于感知的揭示性实验）”，用于揭示原理，未提及用于“训练”，选 NOT GIVEN。

干扰 实验目的在文中是研究/揭示，而非训练。

句子 (Paragraph D) “...people not seeing a hollow face as hollow is the most revealing experiment on perception.”

Q36

解析 题目说**视力完美（perfect vision）**的人也可能无法正确解读所见。原文D段末尾说：“even people with no visual impairment（即使是没有视力障碍的人/视力完美的人）”也会看到他们期望看到的，并经常“miss things as they really are（错过事物的真实面目/无法正确解读）”，选 YES。

干扰 “No visual impairment” 对应 “perfect vision”；“Miss things as they really are” 对应 “fail to interpret correctly”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “The unsettling truth... is that even people with no visual impairment... often miss things as they really are.”

Q37

句子 (Paragraph D) “...the back of the mask will be seen as convex...”

解析 题目说受试者确信他们看到的面具形状是____。原文D段提到，如果面具旋转，背面（back）将被视为“convex（凸起的）”，尽管我们知道它是凹的，对应选项 G (convex)。

干扰 “Seen as ______” 对应 “seen as convex”。

Q38

解析 题目说他们相信____像正常方式一样突出来。原文D段提到正面看是凸起的形状，“with the nose sticking out（鼻子突出来）”，大脑会把背面也脑补成这样，对应选项 F (nose)。

干扰 “Poking out” 对应 “sticking out”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “From the front it is a convex shape with the nose sticking out.”

Q39

解析 题目说试图制作面具的____也会导致同样的问题。原文D段提到几乎不可能“sketch（素描/画）”空心面具的背面让它看起来是空心的，sketch对应选项 I (drawing)。

干扰 “Sketch” 对应 “drawing”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “It is almost... impossible to sketch the back of a hollow mask...”

Q40

解析 题目说受试者没能看到凹陷形状是因为他们有____。原文D段说人们看到的是“they expect to see（他们期望看到的）”，这种期望基于对面部特征突出的知识，expect对应选项 J (preconception)（先入为主/预想）。

干扰 “Expect to see” 对应 “preconception”。

句子 (Paragraph D) “...people... see what, at some level, they expect to see...”
